ai.definition: On-chip AI accelerators are specialized hardware components integrated within microprocessors to enhance the processing capabilities for artificial intelligence and machine learning tasks directly at the device level.
ai.howItWorks: These accelerators offload computationally intensive tasks from the main CPU, allowing for faster and more efficient execution of AI models. They leverage techniques such as tensor operations and specialized hardware designs to optimize performance and reduce power consumption.
ai.problemSolved: Traditional CPUs struggle with the computational demands of modern machine learning algorithms, leading to increased latency and higher energy usage. On-chip AI accelerators address this by providing dedicated processing units that can handle these tasks more efficiently.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing on-chip AI accelerators requires advanced semiconductor fabrication techniques, including the use of specialized materials and processes for integrating high-performance computing elements into existing microprocessor architectures.
ai.buildProcess: The build process involves designing the hardware architecture, implementing machine learning algorithms, and then integrating these components with the rest of the chip. This includes optimizing memory access patterns, managing power consumption, and ensuring compatibility with existing processor designs.
ai.costDrivers: Key cost drivers include the complexity of design, advanced fabrication processes, and the need for high-performance materials. The integration of multiple specialized functions can also increase development time and costs.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is expected to grow as more applications require real-time AI processing at the edge, driving demand and further innovation in design and manufacturing processes.
ai.regulation: Current regulatory frameworks focus on general semiconductor and electronic device standards. Specific regulations for AI accelerators are still developing but may include guidelines related to data privacy and security.
ai.risks: Technological risks include rapid advancements that could render current designs obsolete, while market risks involve competition from established players in the semiconductor industry. Environmental concerns over manufacturing processes also pose a risk.
ai.profitability: Profitability is contingent on market adoption and the ability to reduce costs through economies of scale and technological improvements.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development may focus on improving energy efficiency, expanding support for diverse AI models, and integrating with emerging technologies like quantum computing or neuromorphic hardware.

glossary.def: A specialized hardware component designed to enhance the processing capabilities for artificial intelligence and machine learning tasks.
A distributed computing paradigm that brings data processing closer to the devices generating the data, reducing latency and bandwidth requirements.

subsystems.name: Compute array
subsystems.role: performs the massive parallel multiply-accumulate operations that dominate neural networks.

subsystems.name: On-chip memory hierarchy
subsystems.role: keeps weights and activations close to the compute units so the array is not starved.

subsystems.name: Data movement and interconnect
subsystems.role: moves tensors between memory, compute and the host without consuming too much energy.

subsystems.name: Control and scheduling
subsystems.role: sequences operations and decides what runs when.

subsystems.name: Precision and sparsity support
subsystems.role: trades numerical accuracy for throughput and energy efficiency.

subsystems.name: Host integration
subsystems.role: connects the accelerator to the CPU, memory and external interfaces.
parts: PCIe or chip-to-chip link (for discrete use)

buildSteps.title: Define the architecture
buildSteps.detail: Engineers choose the dataflow (e.g. systolic, weight-stationary), supported precisions and target throughput in operations per second per watt, then model performance in software.

buildSteps.title: Write the register-transfer-level design
buildSteps.detail: The microarchitecture is described in a hardware description language such as Verilog or VHDL and simulated at the cycle level.

buildSteps.title: Verify the design
buildSteps.detail: Testbenches, formal methods and emulation on large FPGA arrays check that the accelerator computes correctly for millions of random and real neural-network inputs.

buildSteps.title: Implement the physical layout
buildSteps.detail: Logic synthesis, place-and-route and timing closure map the design onto standard cells and SRAM blocks in a chosen CMOS node, balancing area, frequency and power.

buildSteps.title: Tape out and make masks
buildSteps.detail: The final layout is sent to a foundry, which writes a set of photomasks — one per layer — for the lithography process.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the wafers
buildSteps.detail: Silicon wafers are processed through hundreds of steps: deposition, photolithography, etching, doping and chemical-mechanical polishing, layer by layer.

buildSteps.title: Package and test
buildSteps.detail: Wafers are diced, known-good dies are packaged (often with DRAM in the same package), and parts are screened for speed, power and defects.

buildSteps.title: Enable the software stack
buildSteps.detail: Compilers, runtimes and drivers map trained models onto the accelerator, scheduling layers and quantising weights so that real applications run at the promised speed.

prerequisites.why: smaller transistors pack more MAC units into a given area and cut switching energy.
the array needs fast local storage for weights and activations to avoid expensive off-chip memory traffic.
8-bit and lower precision lets the same silicon deliver far more inferences per second.

prerequisites.tech: Electronic design automation and verification tools
prerequisites.why: no team can hand-place billions of transistors or prove correctness without them.
stacking or tiling accelerator chiplets with high-bandwidth memory is the main route to larger on-package models.

pathway.milestone: neural processing units integrated into smartphone, PC and embedded processors
pathway.unlocks: real-time speech, camera and sensor inference at a few watts or less.
larger models on device and much lower energy per operation.

pathway.milestone: analog in-memory computing in commercial silicon
pathway.unlocks: matrix multiplication performed where the weights are stored, removing most data movement.
event-driven and light-speed interconnects for always-on and very large models.
